More than most literary genres, SF seems to have a canon of books from the long long ago but everyone references, but I find it hard to believe any actually read, or at least read critically. They introduced some later critical concepts, but as actual reads, they fall shorts.

The two biggest that stand out to me that wind up on 'must read' book lists constantly are -

The Stars My Destination Meandering, nonsensical, relying basically on magic constantly, this one gets hauled out because it introduced the idea of megacorporations and the like. It's even credited as being 'the first cyberpunk novel'. I can give it credit for the concept, but I'd never recommend it.

Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep Let's face it, Philip K. Dick was never at the height of his form in his novels - except perhaps Man in the High Castle - and did much better in his short stories. I'm convinced Electric Sheep only gets on lists is its relationship with Blade Runner, and even then, the two stories barely resemble each other. It lacks everything that made Blade Runner great.

So, what are your candidates for 'classic' books that anyone recommends probably never read?

I think you're just plain wrong about Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep, but given what I'm about to say I don't think I'm in much of a position to judge:

Starship Troopers was better as a movie than it was as a book.

I love both - Verhoeven is my home boy - but I consider them completely separate. Starship Troopers the book was a way of Heinlein to talk about how the military works and explore that, without bringing nationalism into it. Also, the power armor and the talking bomb were brilliant.

Yep. Loved the book - written over 50 years ago, and it's still fresh today - and enjoyed the movie because it was silly and fun.

Don't think it was a great satire though. Verhoeven can't do satire, that takes an element of restraint. Verhoeven does over-the-top parody.
I never felt the film was either satire or parody; I felt it was a straight up homage to WWII propaganda films. It wasn't subtle, but like you said, Verhoeven doesn't do restraint!

I completely disagree with you on Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep. It's a great book, but you can't go into it and expect to read Blade Runner. Movies hardly ever follow their source material, and Blade Runner is no different. The book is not an action story, it's much slower and more emotional.

True. I would only add that Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep was published in 1968 and Blade Runner was released in 1982. So much of what made them both great was the real world events that were taking place around them. Try to study To Kill a Mockingbird or Uncle Tom's Cabin without discussing their historical context. Both are "much less" without the elephant in the room.
